title: PRD (Draft) — Workload-aware batching defaults + SLO tiers (Optimize + Runtime)
linked_artifacts: Confluence:(planned) workload-aware batching defaults design doc
content:
Doc status: EARLY DRAFT (open questions + naming still in flux)
Owner: Aditya Rao (Optimize)
Last edited: 2026-02-02
Reviewers (initial): Nikhil Sharma (Hosted API), Henry Cho (API), Lauren Bishop (Dedicated), Sofia Ivanova (Scheduling), Sean Gallagher (SRE), Allison Grant (Obs)

============================================================
1) Summary / why we’re doing this
============================================================
Batching is one of the highest-leverage runtime knobs for $/1K tokens, but it’s also one of the easiest ways for customers to accidentally create tail-latency regressions (esp. streaming) or overload instabilities.

We will ship three customer-facing “latency SLO tiers” with associated recommended batching profiles:
- fast
- standard
- cost-efficient

The tiers will power:
(A) Runtime defaults (safe, workload-aware, automatically selected when customer does not explicitly set a tier)
(B) Optimize recommendations (advisory + explainability; can suggest tier changes and surface why)

This PRD is specifically focused on the product behavior and UX/contract: what customers see, what they can configure, how Optimize explains and recommends, and what launch criteria look like.

Non-goals in this release:
- Full per-tenant auto-tuning in real time (we will use heuristics and curated profiles; no per-customer closed-loop tuning initially)
- Any major routing-policy redesign (existing routing/fallback policies remain; tier selection is primarily a batching/runtime behavior)

============================================================
2) Goals and success metrics
============================================================
Product goals
- Reduce customer foot-guns: batching “just works” for common workloads without customers reading scheduler docs.
- Provide a simple mental model that lets customers trade cost vs latency in a predictable way.
- Make the system explainable (in Console and via APIs): “what tier is active and why?”
- Enable safe adoption: staged rollout, kill switch, and clear override hierarchy.

Success metrics (initial targets; finalize with SRE)
- Hosted API: measurable reduction in median $/1K tokens (or GPU-seconds / 1K tokens) for workloads that remain within the same latency tier.
- No statistically significant degradation in fast-tier tail latency beyond agreed SLO gates during canary.
- Support: reduction in tickets related to batching misconfiguration; fast resolution path when issues occur.
- Adoption: % of traffic on tiered defaults and/or explicit tier selection; % of Dedicated tenants using overrides.

Guardrail metrics
- Queue depth/queue time regressions (fast tier especially)
- Error rate / overload shedding events
- Telemetry cost regression (tier labels can increase metric cardinality)

============================================================
3) User personas + top user stories
============================================================
Personas
1) API engineer (Hosted API self-serve)
- Wants low operational overhead; picks a tier and moves on.
- Needs a predictable story for streaming chat latency.

2) Platform / infra engineer (Dedicated)
- Wants explicit control and precedence rules.
- Wants to ensure tenant-level overrides don’t break cluster stability.

3) ML engineer / applied team
- Wants to maximize throughput for offline summarization / doc processing.
- Wants understandability + evidence (benchmarks, reason codes).

Top user stories
- As a Hosted API user, I can choose “fast” for a streaming endpoint so user-perceived latency is consistently low.
- As a Hosted API user who does nothing, the system selects a safe tier automatically.
- As a Dedicated operator, I can force a tier at the tenant/cluster/route level and confirm in Console what is actually effective.
- As an Optimize user, I can see “recommended tier” and the reason (traffic pattern, streaming, prompt lengths, concurrency), and I can apply it safely.

============================================================
4) Tier naming (OPEN) + customer messaging
============================================================
Current working names:
- fast
- standard
- cost-efficient

Naming debate (from Product + Eng):
Option A: “fast / standard / cost-efficient”
Pros: simple, intuitive, likely to match expectation.
Cons: “fast” can over-promise; may imply strict realtime guarantees.

Option B: “realtime / balanced / throughput”
Pros: closer to technical tradeoff.
Cons: “realtime” is riskier promise; “throughput” may be interpreted as bulk/offline only.

Option C: “low-latency / balanced / economy”
Pros: less absolute.
Cons: less crisp; “economy” unclear.

Draft guidance (for docs/Console copy)
- We should describe tiers as “default profiles optimized for …” and state that effective latency depends on model, hardware, and request shape.
- We should always show the actual numeric SLO targets separately (per tier), and be explicit about streaming.

Decision needed by: before external docs merge.
Owner: Nikhil + Aditya

============================================================
5) Functional requirements
============================================================
5.1 Tier concept and behavior
- The system exposes a tier parameter (or route policy field) with values: fast | standard | cost-efficient.
- If customer does not set a tier explicitly, runtime selects a default tier based on workload-aware heuristics (inputs TBD by runtime):
  - prompt length distribution (bucketing)
  - streaming vs non-streaming
  - concurrency / arrival rate (coarse)
- Runtime must be able to emit “reason codes” explaining which tier/profile was selected.

5.2 Optimize recommendations vs runtime defaults (critical distinction)
Runtime defaults
- Must be safe and stable under mixed workloads.
- Must prefer predictable tail latency over marginal throughput when in doubt.
- Must degrade gracefully under overload (backpressure / admission control / shedding as appropriate).

Optimize recommendations
- Should be advisory and transparent.
- May recommend:
  - switching tiers (e.g., standard → cost-efficient) for specific routes
  - enabling explicit tier pinning for certain endpoints (esp. streaming)
  - when to use per-route overrides vs leaving workload-aware default selection
- Must show “Why” with evidence: observed traffic shape + expected tradeoff.
- Should avoid recommending changes that violate SLO gates (e.g., recommending cost-efficient for a route that is clearly latency-sensitive and streaming).

Explicit requirements for Optimize
R1. Show current effective tier and source of truth (override hierarchy).
R2. Show recommended tier (if different), plus confidence level.
R3. Show expected impact (directional): latency risk ↑/↓, cost ↓/↑.
R4. Provide an “Apply recommendation” action only where we have safe rollback and policy-scoped changes.
R5. Integrate with observability: after applying, show before/after comparison and warn if regressions detected.

5.3 Override hierarchy and precedence (Hosted vs Dedicated)
We need a deterministic rule. Proposed (align w/ runtime/platform):
1) Customer explicit override at request level (if we allow it; see Open Q)
2) Tenant-level override (Dedicated)
3) Route policy tier (Console / config)
4) Runtime default selection (workload-aware)

Requirements
- Console must display “effective tier” and list which rule applied.
- Audit log must record changes (who/when) for route-level policy changes.

Open Q: request-level tier selection (header/param)
- Pros: debugging + quick experiments; aligns with SDK parameter.
- Cons: can create per-request churn and metric cardinality; can be abused; more support surface.
- If enabled, we likely need to restrict: enterprise-only, allowlist, or rate-limited.

5.4 Streaming-specific requirements
- For streaming endpoints, the user-perceived metric is time-to-first-token (TTFT) and token cadence.
- Fast tier should prioritize TTFT and cadence stability.
- Cost-efficient tier must not introduce pathological streaming chunkiness.

Requirements
- In Console, for streaming routes, show TTFT and p95/p99 on TTFT (not just full request latency).
- Optimize should consider streaming flag as a strong negative signal for cost-efficient unless customer explicitly opts in.

5.5 Observability / explainability requirements (product-visible)
- Customers should see tier usage broken down by:
  - route
  - model
  - region
  - streaming vs non-streaming

- “Why this profile?” UX should include reason codes (examples):
  - DEFAULT_WORKLOAD_HEURISTIC_STREAMING
  - DEFAULT_WORKLOAD_HEURISTIC_LONG_PROMPTS
  - OVERRIDE_ROUTE_POLICY
  - OVERRIDE_DEDICATED_TENANT
  - MODEL_CONSTRAINT_FALLBACK
  - OVERLOAD_MODE_PROTECTION

- Optimize surfaces a simplified version:
  - “We selected Fast because this route is streaming and your p95 TTFT target is tight.”
  - “We recommend Cost-efficient because prompts are short, concurrency is high, and you have margin under Standard SLO.”

============================================================
6) Non-functional requirements
============================================================
Safety
- Must be safe under overload: predictable backpressure and clear error behavior.
- Must prevent starvation in mixed prompt-length workloads.
- Must have kill switch and staged rollout controls.

Compatibility
- Tiers must be compatible with model constraints and (where applicable) quantization profiles.
- If a tier is not supported for a model/hardware combo, system should:
  - pick closest supported tier/profile
  - emit reason code: MODEL_CONSTRAINT_FALLBACK
  - surface warning in Console / logs

Performance / telemetry
- Tier dimension in metrics must be cardinality-safe.
- Avoid exploding labels via per-request tier variability.

============================================================
7) UX / surfaces (early)
============================================================
7.1 Console (proposed)
Where it appears
- Route configuration: “Latency SLO tier” dropdown (fast/standard/cost-efficient) + “Auto (recommended)” option.
- Route details page: “Effective tier” + “Why” + last 24h metrics.
- Optimize page: recommendations list with confidence, expected cost impact, and apply button.

7.2 Public docs
- Explain what each tier means and when to use it.
- Show how to override:
  - per-route policy (primary)
  - Dedicated tenant override (enterprise)
  - request-level (if supported)
- Include FAQ: “What if I don’t pick a tier?”

7.3 SDK/API ergonomics (hosted)
- If supported, allow parameter: batching_tier=fast|standard|cost_efficient.
- Must be consistent across Python/TS.
- Must be validated and return useful errors.

Open Q: naming convention in API
- cost-efficient vs cost_efficient (snake case)
- Ensure docs match.

============================================================
8) Rollout plan (product perspective)
============================================================
Stages (align with runtime release plan)
1) Internal canary (Redwood-owned traffic + perf canary gating)
2) Hosted API: limited cohort (opt-in or allowlist) + kill switch
3) Dedicated: opt-in for selected tenants with known traffic patterns
4) Default-on (Hosted), then broader Dedicated enablement

Launch criteria (draft)
- Perf canary gates green for fast-tier p99 and standard-tier p95 for top models/regions.
- Error budget impact within thresholds.
- Tier metrics dashboards live with paging thresholds agreed.
- Support playbook and docs FAQ complete.

Comms
- Release notes: emphasize “defaults are safer” + “you can override per route.”
- Avoid claiming universal latency improvements; frame as “more predictable.”

============================================================
9) Open questions / decisions needed
============================================================
Q1: Final tier names
Owner: Nikhil + Aditya
Due: before docs PR merge

Q2: Should customers be able to set tier per request?
- Potential enterprise-only feature.
- Alternative: allow for a short-lived debugging token / header.
Owner: Henry + Platform (Priya/Ethan) + SRE

Q3: What is the default behavior if user does nothing?
Options:
- Always standard
- Workload-aware selection (streaming -> fast; bulk -> cost-efficient)
We need a crisp statement for docs.
Owner: Runtime (Sofia) + Product

Q4: How do we avoid “tier sprawl” as we add hardware/model-specific profiles?
We should keep customer surface area fixed at 3 tiers; complexity stays internal.
But we need to confirm how we message “same tier behaves slightly differently across models/hardware.”
Owner: Aditya + Evals

Q5: Optimize confidence + safety scoring
- What do we base confidence on? (traffic volume, stability of workload signals)
- When do we show “insufficient data”?
Owner: Optimize + Observability

Q6: Dedicated override UX and precedence clarity
We’ve seen confusion historically when route policy conflicts with tenant override.
Need explicit “override active” badges.
Owner: Lauren + Console (Dylan/Chloe)

============================================================
10) Appendix: draft tier positioning (NON-NORMATIVE)
============================================================
Fast
- Best for: interactive chat, streaming UX, tight tail latency.
- Tradeoff: higher $/token.

Standard
- Best for: most workloads; balanced latency/cost.

Cost-efficient
- Best for: offline, summarization, batch-like workloads, high concurrency.
- Tradeoff: higher latency and more variance; may be unsuitable for streaming unless customer opts in.

============================================================
11) Notes / next actions
============================================================
- Schedule PRD review #1 (30 min) with Runtime + SRE + Hosted API PMs.
- Collect data points from perf suite: what are the initial candidate profiles for top model families?
- Draft Console copy for “Auto (recommended)” and “Why this profile?”
- Decide policy on request-level tier parameter.

Changelog
- 2026-01-08: initial draft created (Aditya)
- 2026-01-21: added override hierarchy + per-request tier open Q (Henry feedback)
- 2026-02-02: expanded Optimize requirements and streaming-specific metrics (Nikhil + SRE feedback)
